NASA says Voyager 1 has reached one light-day from Earth
 0 
 By
 Editorial Team 
 on 
 November 20, 2026 
 Aeronautics & Aircraft , Featured Stories , Space Exploration , Virtual Reality 
 NASA says Voyager 1, the agency’s longest-operating and most distant spacecraft, reached a distance of one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026, marking a milestone nearly five decades after its 1977 launch.
 A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometres). NASA said the spacecraft reached the threshold at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) on Nov. 18.
 Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California heard from the probe about 24 hours later, which is the time it takes for the spacecraft’s radio signal to travel back to Earth. NASA said the milestone was confirmed using the spacecraft’s carrier signal and trajectory calculations.
 The agency said it has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, although the spacecraft continues transmitting a carrier signal that typically carries that data. Engineers are continuing to analyse the issue affecting the data stream.
 Launched in 1977 alongside Voyager 2 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment, the two probes were sent to explore the outer solar system. NASA said the spacecraft were the third and fourth to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery. Voyager 2 later continued to Uranus and Neptune.
 NASA said both spacecraft remain in interstellar space, with Voyager 1 having crossed the heliosphere boundary in 2012 and Voyager 2 doing so in 2018. The probes continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances.
 The update also highlighted ongoing efforts to manage the constraints of aging hardware and limited power. NASA said both probes lose about 4 watts of power each year as their radioisotope thermal generators decline, and that recent energy-saving work is expected to keep the current suite of science instruments operating until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer.
 NASA said communications with both probes are handled by the agency’s Deep Space Network, a set of large antennas located at three facilities worldwide. At the current distance, NASA said signals take about 24 hours to reach Voyager 1 and 24 hours to return to Earth.
